summary: Find partial erasers that do WIDTH-AWARE REGION SUBTRACTION (semicircle side-bites), not centerline splitting

candidates.name: fabric.js EraserBrush / @erase2d/fabric (ShaMan123)
candidates.evidence: GEOMETRY = YES it can take a shallow one-edge bite. It never touches the stroke polygon; it accumulates the eraser path into a per-object ClippingGroup assigned as that object's clipPath (SVG <mask> on export). Because a clip mask can occlude ANY sub-region, a shallow scallop on one edge of a thick stroke works and the rest of the width stays visible. Source: packages/fabric/src/EraserBrush.ts commitErasing() adds the drawn path to the object's ClippingGroup and marks clipPath+object dirty; README states 'the main context is clipped by the brush, and the top context is masked with relevant objects.' It is the ONLY candidate here that ships a hosted, no-login, one-click eraser demo the rig can drive directly (https://shaman123.github.io/erase2d/, PR #7470 'EraserBrush V2').
candidates.robustness: Sidesteps the boolean-sliver problem entirely — no polygon subtraction, no martinez, so no 'holeOf' crashes, no degenerate zero-area rings, no thin crescents. The cost is the opposite failure: the mask is an ever-growing ClippingGroup (one path appended per erase gesture, never merged/simplified), so heavy erasing bloats object state and slows re-render. No min-area cull needed because nothing is subtracted; the tradeoff is unbounded mask accumulation.
candidates.exportModel: Does NOT yield a subtracted vector stroke. toObject() serializes a clipPath/eraser sub-object; toSVG() emits a <mask>/<clipPath>. The original full-width stroke geometry is intact underneath the mask. For our PDF /InkList export this is the wrong shape: there is no carved outline to write — we'd have to rasterize the masked result, or re-derive the visible geometry ourselves (defeating the point). Good for a live in-app eraser feel, poor as a source of exportable carved ink.
candidates.notes: Fabric 7 is our stack already (see CLAUDE.md fabric-7 gotchas). Lowest-risk way to get the VISUAL side-bite fast, but it is a mask, not true region subtraction — flag if PDF ink fidelity on export matters. This is the 'looks right, may bloat' archetype the brief calls out.
candidates.skepticReason: Primary source EraserBrush.ts commitErasing() confirms erasing = appending the eraser path to a per-object ClippingGroup assigned as clipPath (mask); object geometry/path points are never modified, never split, never deleted. Render is destination-out clip compositing and toSVG emits an SVG <mask> (vector, not raster). A clip mask can occlude any arbitrary sub-region, so dragging along one edge of a thick stroke masks a shallow scallop while the rest of the width stays visible = a genuine side-bite. Classification mask-clip-sidebite is correct; not centerline-split, not raster, not whole-delete. Hosted no-login demo (shaman123.github.io/erase2d) verified. Caveat: exports as SVG mask over untouched original stroke, not a clean modified vector stroke, so it does not directly give PDF /InkList.

candidates.name: Paper.js vector eraser (offsetPath + path.subtract, beardicus gist)
candidates.evidence: GEOMETRY = YES, true one-edge bite. On mouseup it builds the eraser stroke's outline with OffsetUtils.offsetPath() (inner+outer offsets united with round end-caps = a swept capsule/disk region), then calls path.subtract() of that region from each overlapping FILLED target path, leaving a scalloped concave remainder. During drag it only fakes it with a blend-mode mask, committing real vector subtraction on release. This is exactly the target model (boolean subtract of a swept disk from a filled stroke body). Confirmed against gist source + paperjs.org/reference/path (#subtract, options.trace treating both as areas).
candidates.robustness: This is the weak point. Paper.js's built-in boolean engine is NOT hardened for this: documented failures include subtract producing OPEN paths (issue #968), overlapping curves left in the result as a CompoundPath (issue #661), and general subtraction glitches (#419). The gist only mitigates with path.simplify(); there is no min-area sliver cull, no SDF/raster intermediate, no Minkowski. Expect exactly the thin-crescent / degenerate-ring problems the brief fears. If we adopt this model, do NOT trust Paper's native booleans — swap in a better clipper + explicit min-area cull.
candidates.exportModel: Keeps VECTOR (a Paper Path/CompoundPath), good — but note it operates on the FILLED stroke body, so the result is a filled outline region, not a centerline+width stroke. To write PDF /InkList we'd re-fit the carved outline; more naturally this exports as a filled path (/AP appearance stream) than as InkList. Converts stroke -> filled outline.
candidates.notes: No hosted eraser demo, but the gist pastes straight into sketch.paperjs.org (no login) so the rig can drive it. Best reference for the target ALGORITHM; its boolean lib is the liability, not the approach.
candidates.skepticReason: Refuted against verbatim gist source (https://gist.github.com/beardicus/8cbe9511d43e3fb58d76e336f76f4eb2). Two decisive facts contradict the claim: (1) Target artwork is a STROKED open centerline path (new Path with strokeColor/strokeWidth, no fillColor, not closed) — NOT a filled stroke body as claimed. Width is a render attribute, not geometry. (2) The commit uses item.subtract(deleteShape, { trace: false }). Per paperjs.org PathItem reference, trace:false does NOT treat operands as areas — it only splits the first path at intersections and keeps curve pieces outside, so the boolean acts on the zero-width centerline. Result: each piece keeps full strokeWidth; grazing only the rim of a thick stroke intersects no centerline and removes nothing, while reaching the centerline severs the full width. That is centerline-interval-split (same class as js-draw PartialStroke/Xournal++/Rnote/MS GetEraseResult) — the WRONG model. It can never carve a shallow one-edge bite. The scalloped 'side-bite look' during drag is a transient source-out blend-mode MASK, explicitly discarded on mouseup per the README, replaced by the centerline-split commit. The claim's assertion 'options.trace treating both as areas' and 'FILLED target path' is directly contradicted by the source. Note: the offsetPath capsule builder is the right ingredient and WOULD give region-subtraction if applied to a filled path with trace:true, but the gist as written does neither.

candidates.robustness: mfogel/polygon-clipping is the more robust, better-maintained successor to martinez (it was written to fix martinez precision/robustness bugs) — so it avoids the specific martinez 'holeOf' crash class. It is NOT sliver-proof on its own: subtracting a disk sweep still breeds thin crescents and near-zero-area rings, so we still must add a min-area/thin-ness cull and snap-rounding after difference(). No built-in SDF/raster fallback. This is the 'bring your own robustness' option — most control, most work.
candidates.exportModel: Filled outline polygon (MultiPolygon rings). Not a native centerline stroke. Clean to convert to a PDF filled appearance; for /InkList you'd sample the outline. Same 'stroke -> filled outline' tradeoff as Paper.js but with a stronger clipper.
candidates.notes: The Vercel playground only draws (no eraser), so the side-bite itself isn't pre-built to drive — but this is the recommended BUILD path: perfect-freehand for stroke bodies we already suit, polygon-clipping.difference() for the carve, plus our own sliver cull. Strongest target-model foundation of the set.
candidates.skepticReason:
CONFIRMED as region-subtraction-sidebite by construction — the skeptic pass fails to refute it. Both primary claims verify:

(1) perfect-freehand getStroke() returns a FILLED OUTLINE polygon, NOT a centerline. README (github.com/steveruizok/perfect-freehand): "getStroke will return a new array of outline points... [that] form a polygon (called a 'stroke') that surrounds the input points," rendered via Path2D + ctx.fill / SVG fill. So the stroke has genuine 2D width as a closed polygon — the precondition for side-biting.

(2) mfogel/polygon-clipping exposes difference(subjectGeom, ...clipGeoms) on Polygon/MultiPolygon with hole support, output "always a MultiPolygon containing one or more non-overlapping...Polygons," empty result = []. difference(strokeOutlinePoly, eraserSweepCapsule) is a true boolean area subtraction.

GEOMETRY VERDICT: It genuinely carves a shallow one-edge bite. Boolean polygon difference removes exactly the overlap region. When a small eraser disk/capsule sweep overlaps only the RIM of a thick stroke, the difference leaves a concave scalloped notch on that edge while the rest of the stroke width survives untouched — a shallow semicircle/scallop bite, bite depth = eraser radius. It does NOT full-width sever on contact. It severs into two pieces only when the swept disk spans the entire stroke width (naturally emitted as a 2-polygon MultiPolygon). This is precisely the Drawboard target model and the OPPOSITE of centerline-split (js-draw PartialStroke / Xournal++ / Rnote), which delete full width the instant the eraser touches the centerline and can never take a side-bite. Refutation attempts (full-width sever / raster-paint / whole-delete) all FAIL — none apply here. tldraw/excalidraw lineage claim is accurate: this perfect-freehand + polygon boolean stack is the real DIY pattern.

ROBUSTNESS (the notorious weakness — real and unsolved in this exact lib): mfogel/polygon-clipping is martinez-derived and crashes on floating-point sweep-line round-off — open/recurring "Unable to find segment #N in SweepLine tree. Please submit a bug report." on difference()/union() (issues #60, #98, #115, #148; #148 notes a fix that regressed at v0.14.0). The library ships only blunt guards (POLYGON_CLIPPING_MAX_QUEUE_SIZE / MAX_SWEEPLINE_SEGMENTS env caps) to abort infinite loops, no snap-rounding, and is effectively unmaintained. It has NO built-in min-area sliver cull or degenerate-ring cleanup — the thin crescent/zero-area-ring problem is on the caller to solve (coordinate snapping + post-difference min-area filter). So the DIY stack IS the right MODEL (region-subtraction-sidebite) but mfogel/polygon-clipping is a fragile clipper choice; a hardened build would swap to a snap-rounding/integer clipper (e.g. Clipper2/polygon-clipping-forks or an SDF-raster intermediate) and add sliver culling.

EXPORT: getStroke() output is already a filled polygon, not a native stroked centerline — after boolean difference the geometry is a filled outline MultiPolygon, so exporting to PDF /InkList requires either re-fitting a centerline+width to each surviving piece (lossy) or exporting the filled outline as a path appearance stream. This stack does NOT preserve a clean vector centerline through the erase — a real consideration for the /InkList export requirement.

candidates.robustness: Excellent for on-screen (no boolean lib, so no martinez 'holeOf' crashes, no slivers). The cost is moved to EXPORT, not eliminated.

EraserBrush extends fabric.PencilBrush (freehand) and renders with globalCompositeOperation 'destination-out', removing only the pixels the brush physically passes over. Commit does not modify stroke path points; instead commitErasing() adds the eraser path into a ClippingGroup on the object's clipPath (README: 'clips the entire canvas and masks all non-erasable objects'). Boolean-difference that filled polygon against the swept eraser disk (a capsule/Minkowski sum of the eraser circle along its drag path) => a shallow concave bite out of one edge, rest of width intact. Sources: https://www.npmjs.com/package/perfect-freehand , https://github.com/steveruizok/perfect-freehand (issue #94 on cleaning path data), boolean lib https://github.com/mfogel/polygon-clipping .
candidates.exportModel: Converts the stroke to a FILLED OUTLINE polygon (MultiPolygon), NOT a centerline. For PDF you'd export it as a filled path, OR re-fit a centerline+width to write /InkList — non-trivial if a bite makes the width non-uniform. This is the key export trade-off to decide up front.
candidates.robustness: Use Clipper2, NOT martinez. Clipper2 runs boolean ops on INTEGER coordinates and, per its own robustness docs, splits results and 'discards smaller polygons with negligible area' — i.e. built-in sliver/degenerate-ring culling, exactly the failure the target model is notorious for. martinez-polygon-clipping is double-precision float and documented as 'not robust' (this is the lib that throws the 'holeOf' crash). Add your own min-area cull + snap-rounding on top. Sources: https://www.angusj.com/clipper2/Docs/Robustness.htm , https://www.angusj.com/clipper2/Docs/Overview.htm , JS/WASM binding e.g. clipper2-js / clipper2-wasm.
candidates.notes: No turnkey playground for the ERASE step — it's a toolkit, the rig can't 'drive' it. But it's the only open path that yields honest vector geometry AND solvable robustness (Clipper2 min-area cull + Minkowski capsule sweep). Recommended engine for the persistent/commit layer, paired with a Fabric or SVG live preview.

candidates.skepticReason:
CONFIRMED as region-subtraction-sidebite MECHANISM, with a load-bearing correction the claim omits. Primary source (src/ui/tools/eraser-tool.cpp) verifies every mechanical assertion: _brush() builds a genuine width-aware ribbon (point1=brush+del_left, point2=brush-del_right, perpendicular to velocity via rot90(vel)); _completeBezier() fits BOTH edges with Geom::bezier_fit_cubic_r; _accumulate() closes the ribbon (accumulated.append(rev_cal2); accumulated.close()); _addCap() adds rounded caps; and CUT mode applies a real 2D boolean: nowidth=(width==0); if(nowidth) operands.pathCut(true,true) else operands.pathDiff(true,true). With eraser width>0 this is a true boolean DIFFERENCE of the swept-disk ribbon, so dragging the edge carves a concave scalloped side-bite and leaves the rest intact. It is NOT centerline-split as its primary mechanism (pathCut only fires in the width==0 degenerate case), NOT raster, NOT whole-delete.

CRITICAL CORRECTION (why the claim is misleading for OUR use case): pathDiff operates on the target's FILL geometry only. There is NO stroke-to-path/outline conversion before the boolean; _handleStrokeStyle() only preserves the even-odd fill rule, it does not expand stroke-width into a body. So the difference does NOT respect a target's stroke-width. Therefore: (a) on a genuinely FILLED thick shape — including Inkscape Calligraphy-tool ink, which is stored as a FILLED path, not a stroke — the side-bite works perfectly (this is the true target behavior); (b) on a raw STROKED open path with no fill (Pencil/Bezier ink, i.e. exactly our pen/highlighter /InkList export target), pathDiff runs on empty/degenerate fill geometry and does NOT bite the visible thick stroke — it produces nothing useful, or with width==0 severs the centerline. The claim's phrase 'the filled stroke body' is precisely the gap: Inkscape assumes the body is ALREADY filled; it never outlines a stroke for you.

So Inkscape IS a valid region-subtraction-sidebite reference, but only when ink is represented as a filled outline. To reuse this model for /InkList we must stroke->outline first, subtract, then re-fit a centerline on export. Robustness: sliver/degenerate defense is at the filter stage (_filterCutEraseables rejects raster + zero-area paths; _filterByCollision/collidesWith bbox-prefilters); boolean engine is 2geom/livarot, not martinez. Export model: filled vector SVG paths (not centerline ink). Source: https://gitlab.com/inkscape/inkscape/-/raw/master/src/ui/tools/eraser-tool.cpp

Verified from cloned primary source (index.html): erasable ink is a thin OPEN centerline `new Path({strokeColor, strokeWidth})` with no fill — never converted to a filled stroke-body outline. The eraser does build a real filled swept-capsule region (deleteShape via OffsetUtils offset both sides + endcaps + unite), but the operation is `item.subtract(deleteShape, {trace:false})` on the thin centerline. Paper.js primary source (src/path/PathItem.Boolean.js): subtract with trace:false routes to splitBoolean(), which divides path1 at its intersections with path2 and keeps whole sub-segments via a midpoint containment test (`_path2.contains(path.getPointAt(len/2)) ^ subtract`) — operating on curve GEOMETRY ONLY; strokeWidth is never read (boolean ops are geometry-only by design). Consequence: grazing the edge of a thick stroke without crossing its centerline yields ZERO intersections → stroke untouched (no bite); crossing the centerline removes the full width over that interval and severs into pieces (the code's result.children/insertChildren branch handles exactly these multi-piece splits, and the author's comment concedes it needs open/closed detection). It can never carve a shallow one-edge bite. The convincing-looking side-shave is the real-time canvas source-out blend MASK preview, which is ephemeral and discarded on mouseUp; committed geometry is the centerline split. Corrected eraseModel: centerline-split. A true sidebite would require storing ink as a filled closed stroke-body outline, which this gist does not do.

candidates.name: Fabric.js EraserBrush (@erase2d/fabric, ShaMan123)
candidates.evidence: Erases via canvas globalCompositeOperation on a clip mask, not geometry boolean. The brush draws the eraser path with 'destination-out' and, on commit, accumulates it into each object's clipPath as a ClippingGroup: clipPath.add(sourceInObjectPlane); it replaces an existing clip with new ClippingGroup([existingClipPath]). Because the removed swath is exactly the eraser's own round-cap stroke width, dragging over the edge of a thick stroke visually shaves a side-bite — VISUALLY right. Source: https://github.com/ShaMan123/erase2d/blob/master/packages/fabric/src/EraserBrush.ts ; docs https://www.npmjs.com/package/@erase2d/fabric ; classic demo https://fabric5.fabricjs.com/erasing .
candidates.robustness: No sliver/boolean-crash risk at all — it never does polygon subtraction, it composites pixels through an accumulating clipPath. The cost is BLOAT/opacity: every erase stroke is appended to a ClippingGroup that grows unboundedly, so long editing sessions accumulate large clip trees and re-render cost climbs; there is no geometric simplification of the mask. This is exactly the 'visually right, may bloat' failure mode.

candidates.name: perfect-freehand + polygon-clipping / Clipper2 (build-your-own)
candidates.evidence: Not a shipping eraser but the canonical RECIPE for the target: perfect-freehand getStroke() turns input points into a FILLED polygon OUTLINE (spline points -> outline points), and its own docs tell you to run polygonClipping.union([stroke]) to flatten self-crossings before rendering. Once the stroke body is a filled polygon, an eraser bite is polygonClipping.difference(strokePoly, eraserSweepPoly) — a real width-aware side-bite. Source: https://github.com/steveruizok/perfect-freehand (README 'Flattening', getStroke, getSvgPathFromStroke).
candidates.robustness: polygon-clipping (mfogel, martinez-derived) is the weak link — it throws the notorious 'holeOf'/segment errors on near-degenerate input and is not numerically robust. Recommended fix: use Clipper2 (AngusJohnson) instead, which clips in INTEGER coordinates internally (ClipperD scales/de-scales by a decimal precision) for numerical robustness, plus offsetting for the eraser capsule; then min-area cull the difference result. Clipper2 robustness note: https://angusj.com/clipper2/Docs/Robustness.htm ; martinez non-robustness confirmed at https://github.com/w8r/martinez .
candidates.exportModel: Filled outline (perfect-freehand already emits outline polygons). Natural fit for /AP appearance-stream export; not a native centerline /InkList.
candidates.eraseCodePointers: perfect-freehand: getStroke() returns outline point ring; README shows getSvgPathFromStroke + polygonClipping.union([stroke]). Difference/subtract is the eraser step you add.
candidates.notes: This is effectively how to BUILD the Drawboard behavior cleanly. Pair getStroke outline with Clipper2 difference + sliver cull. The demo playground has no eraser but proves the outline generation the rig can drive.
candidates.skepticReason: CONFIRMED as region-subtraction-sidebite. Primary sources verify the full chain: perfect-freehand README states getStroke() returns outline points forming a filled polygon (real 2D width, not a centerline), and its "Flattening" section directs users to polygon-clipping's union to clean self-crossings; polygon-clipping README confirms a difference() op (Martinez-Rueda) that subtracts one polygon region from another. Because difference operates on the filled 2D area, an eraser sweep overlapping only one edge removes only that overlap and leaves the rest of the width intact = a true concave/scalloped one-edge bite. It is vector (not raster), partial (not whole-delete), and area-based (never full-width centerline-sever), so all three REFUTE hypotheses fail. Caveats that qualify but do not overturn the model: (1) it is a build-your-own RECIPE — the README describes flattening only, never erasing, so there is no shipping/tested eraser. (2) Robustness is the known weak spot: polygon-clipping (Martinez-Rueda) openly warns of round-off infinite loops mitigated only by MAX_QUEUE_SIZE/MAX_SWEEPLINE_SEGMENTS caps — the exact sliver/degenerate-ring/crash family flagged; the robust half of the claim is Clipper2 (integer coords) + min-area cull, NOT raw polygon-clipping (they are not interchangeable). (3) Export mismatch: after difference the stroke is a filled-outline polygon, not a vector centerline+width stroke, so it does not round-trip to PDF /InkList without re-fitting a centerline — natural export is a filled /AP appearance path.

This is width-aware nibbling, not whole-sever. No public statement of the underlying algorithm or latency. Sources: https://www.drawboard.com/blog/how-to-use-the-pen-eraser , https://support.drawboard.com/hc/en-us/articles/4406219880463 .

Structural evidence points the other way: (1) "segments" = intervals along a polyline, the centerline-split signature — a true region-subtract dragged lengthwise would hollow a channel/leave rails, not produce segments; (2) Drawboard's own bug note ("partially erasing same ink twice… duplicated ink on move") shows results remain editable ink objects, i.e. shorter full-width sub-strokes, not arbitrary concave filled polygons; (3) PDF /InkList (points + uniform width) structurally cannot encode a concave edge bite, so a tool keeping editable ink can only split the centerline; (4) Drawboard PDF's Windows Ink heritage ties it to GetEraseResult, which the task itself classifies as centerline-split. Closed-source, paid, no public no-login playground to drive, no video of a thick-stroke edge scallop found — cannot be behaviorally confirmed. Corrected model: centerline-split (WRONG-model contrast entry). Verdict is evidence-based inference, not a driven observation; would flip only on a demonstration of a concave edge scallop stored as a filled path rather than /InkList.

Docs describe Precision, Standard, Stroke erasers; the Standard eraser 'erases chunks of a line rather than whole lines' and Precision is 'for small details ... cleaning up individual lines or flaws' — i.e. partial-width nibble, distinct from the whole-line Stroke eraser. candidates.skepticReason: GoodNotes primary docs describe the Standard Eraser as erasing "chunks of a line, leaving the new stroke endings in the same style as the Pen style you were using." Generating new pen-style endcaps means the stroke is severed across its FULL WIDTH at the eraser-contact interval and re-capped — the signature of centerline/interval splitting, not a concave side-bite. "Chunks of a line" removes intervals along the stroke's length, not slivers across its width. Precision Eraser is only a smaller radius / finer granularity, not a different geometric model; Stroke Eraser deletes whole vector strokes on touch, confirming vector-stroke substrate. Corroborated by the general split-at-intersection algorithm (US9916017B2). No evidence of disk-sweep polygon subtraction from a filled stroke body; the pen-style re-capping is incompatible with edge-nibbling region subtraction. Also fails suitability preferences: closed-source, native iPad/macOS, no public browser playground, proprietary export. Corrected model: centerline-split.

candidates.name: Notability (Partial eraser)
candidates.evidence: FAMILY. Two modes: Partial eraser vs Whole eraser ('Entire strokes can be erased at once with the Whole Eraser'), so the Partial mode by definition removes sub-stroke portions. Source: https://support.gingerlabs.com/hc/en-us/articles/360029432891-Eraser .
candidates.robustness: Undocumented.

candidates.notes: iOS/macOS only, no browser build. Behavioral match but not drivable by a web rig.
candidates.skepticReason: Primary sources refute region-subtraction-sidebite. Ginger Labs' own vector-graphics engineering blog states the Partial Eraser uses the Bézier Clipping curve-intersection algorithm to 'split objects apart' into 'newly subdivided objects' — path-vs-path (centerline) intersection producing severed pieces, the centerline-split signature. Ginger Labs support confirms each resulting segment retains an editable scalar 'width' attribute (stroked-centerline + width representation, not a filled outline polygon), so a per-segment scalar width cannot carry a one-edge crescent bite. A technical description confirms contact detection is proximity to the centerline with 'threshold depends on stroke width' (halfWidth+eraserRadius), and the documented user failure mode is 'cutting entire lines,' fixed by a smaller eraser to remove shorter intervals ALONG the path — never trimming a thick line's width from one side. No evidence of shallow edge-nibbling anywhere. The claim's FAMILY logic (two modes → sub-stroke removal) only rules out whole-only; it cannot distinguish centerline-split from side-bite, and the evidence lands squarely on centerline-split. The cited US20200372208 patent is Microsoft's (a centerline-split contrast), not Ginger Labs. Notability is closed-source with no public browser playground, so not a rig target.

candidates.name: Clipper2 (AngusJohnson) — robustness backbone, not an eraser
candidates.evidence: Included as the ROBUSTNESS answer for building the target. Clipper2 does difference/union/intersection/XOR plus polygon offsetting; Clipper64/ClipperD clip using INTEGER coordinates internally for numerical robustness (ClipperD scales/de-scales by a set decimal precision). This is the clean way to subtract the eraser capsule (offset of the eraser polyline) from the perfect-freehand stroke outline without martinez 'holeOf' crashes. Docs: https://angusj.com/clipper2/Docs/Robustness.htm , https://github.com/AngusJohnson/Clipper2 . JS port: clipper2-js / clipper2-wasm.
candidates.robustness: Integer-coordinate clipping (robust); InflatePaths() gives the eraser-disk/capsule via Minkowski-style offsetting so you never hand-build the sweep polygon; add a min-area cull on Difference() output to drop sliver crescents.
candidates.exportModel: Emits filled outline polygons -> /AP appearance stream export.
candidates.notes: Not a shipping eraser or playground; the recommended engine under a Paper.js/perfect-freehand-style implementation to beat the sliver/degenerate-ring/boolean-crash problems.
candidates.skepticReason: Clipper2 primary docs confirm it does Difference/Union/Intersection/XOR plus InflatePaths offsetting on arbitrary filled polygons, using integer coordinates internally for robustness (predictable +/-1 imprecision, orientation-reversal polygon splitting, negligible-area/sliver culling of edges under 2 units, ClipperD scale/de-scale by precision). Critically, Clipper2 has NO concept of stroke/line-width/centerline (stated verbatim on Overview.htm), so centerline-split is impossible by construction — there is no centerline to sever. Fed Difference(filled perfect-freehand stroke outline, eraser capsule from InflatePaths of the eraser polyline) where the capsule overlaps only one edge, exact boolean geometry yields a concave scallop side-bite with the rest of the width intact; a full-width sever occurs only if the capsule is made to span the full width, which is an input-geometry choice, not a forced model. It is vector integer clipping, not raster, and returns the residual region, not deletion. Refutations as centerline-split/raster/whole all fail. Only nuance: Clipper2 is the boolean+offset engine ('robustness backbone, not an eraser'), not an eraser with its own eraseModel — but that is exactly how the claim frames it, so region-subtraction-sidebite (enabling engine) stands.
